title: IELTS Academic Reading Practice Test 47
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Answer all questions.

passages.title: Selling Winter
passages.text:
A. Before anyone could manufacture cold, it was harvested. Ice was cut from frozen lakes and rivers in winter, stored in insulated houses through the summer, and shipped to places that had never experienced a frost, and for several decades this was a substantial international trade in a commodity that consisted of nothing but water and the labour of moving it before it disappeared.

B. The business rested on a physical fact that is easy to miss. A large block of ice melts slowly because the volume that stores cold grows faster than the surface that admits heat, so a sufficiently large stack, well insulated with sawdust, loses only its outer portion over a long voyage. The economics were built on geometry: the trade was viable at scale and impossible in small quantities.

C. Demand had to be manufactured before it could be met. In places where nobody had used ice, there was no habit of chilled drinks, no equipment to store it, and no reason to buy it, so early shipments went unsold and rotted, and the trade grew only where merchants gave ice away to bartenders and doctors until a dependence formed. The market was created deliberately, at a loss, over years.

D. What the ice changed most was not comfort but food. Reliable cold allowed fish, meat and dairy to travel further and keep longer, which extended the area a city could draw its food from and altered what people ate; it also permitted the storage of surpluses that had previously been wasted. The luxury use in drinks was visible and the significant use was in the supply chain behind them.

E. Mechanical refrigeration destroyed the trade with unusual speed, and the sequence is instructive. Manufactured ice was initially more expensive and was bought anyway, because it could be made in summer, made near the customer, and made without depending on the severity of a distant winter — advantages that mattered more than price. Reliability displaced a cheaper product, as it often does.

F. The industry left an infrastructure that outlived its purpose. Ice houses, insulated wagons, cold stores and the trades that built and ran them existed before mechanical cooling and were adapted to it rather than replaced, so the physical network of the cold chain was inherited rather than invented. The systems that now move chilled food follow routes and use buildings established by a trade in frozen lake water.

passages.title: The Bite and the Cure
passages.text:
Venom is not a single substance but a mixture, typically of dozens of proteins, and its complexity is what makes treating envenoming so difficult. Different components attack different systems — some destroy tissue, some prevent blood from clotting, some cause it to clot uncontrollably, some block the signals between nerve and muscle — and the mixture differs between species, between populations of the same species, and sometimes between an adult and a juvenile of the same population.

The treatment has changed remarkably little in principle since it was devised. An animal, usually a horse or a sheep, is injected with small quantities of venom until its immune system produces antibodies, and those antibodies are extracted and purified for injection into a bitten person. It is effective, it is one of the older biological medicines still in routine use, and it carries the risks that come from injecting proteins from another species.

The specificity problem follows directly from venom's variability. An antivenom raised against one species may work poorly or not at all against another, so a product effective in one region may be useless a few hundred kilometres away, and treatment depends on identifying what bit the patient — often from a description given by someone in severe distress, at night, who did not see the animal clearly. Broader products covering several species exist and require larger doses.

The economics have failed in a way that is not really about medicine. The people bitten are overwhelmingly rural agricultural workers in low-income regions, they cannot pay much, the product is expensive to make and requires refrigeration and skilled administration, and manufacturers have withdrawn from markets that could not sustain the cost. A treatment that works has become unavailable in the places that need it, which is a distribution failure rather than a scientific one.

Counterfeit and substandard products fill the gap left behind, with predictable results. Where effective antivenom is unavailable or unaffordable, products with little or no active content are sold, and their failure is attributed to the severity of the bite rather than to the medicine, so the market does not correct itself. The presence of something on the shelf also removes the political pressure that an obvious absence would create.

What would improve outcomes most is not a better antivenom. Reliable supply of the products that already work, refrigeration in rural clinics, staff trained to administer them and to manage the reactions, and transport that gets a patient to a clinic within hours would save more lives than any pharmaceutical advance now in development. The problem has been solved and not delivered, which describes a great deal of global health.

passages.title: After the Water Goes Down
passages.text:
Recovery from a disaster is studied far less than response to one, and the imbalance shapes what is funded. The dramatic phase — rescue, shelter, emergency supplies — attracts attention, money and personnel, and it lasts days or weeks; the recovery phase determines whether a place returns to something like its previous condition, lasts years, and is largely invisible. Most of the money and nearly all of the coverage go to the shorter, more visible half.

Rebuilding tends to reproduce the vulnerability that caused the damage. Pressure to restore quickly, ownership patterns that fix where things must be rebuilt, and the absence of the money required for anything better mean that housing is often replaced as it was, in the place it was, to the standard it was — and the next event finds the same buildings in the same place. Doing it differently costs more at exactly the moment when least is available.

The distribution of recovery is more unequal than the distribution of damage. Households with savings, insurance, secure title and the documentation to prove it recover substantially faster than those without, and assistance programmes typically require exactly the paperwork that poorer households lack. A disaster that damaged a district evenly can leave it, several years later, considerably more unequal than it was.

Aid that arrives as goods rather than money frequently does harm that is easy to miss. Donated food and clothing arriving in quantity displaces local traders and producers at the moment they are trying to restart, so the shops that would have re-established themselves do not, and the local economy's recovery is delayed by the assistance. Cash transfers, where markets are functioning, consistently outperform goods on almost every measure that has been examined.

Insurance and aid interact in a way that discourages preparation. Where losses are reliably covered after the event by government assistance, the incentive to insure or to build more robustly falls, since the cost of caution is borne privately and the cost of damage is shared — and the assistance is difficult to withhold once the damage is visible and the people affected are on television. Announcing that no help will come is not credible, and everyone involved knows it.

The interventions with the best evidence are all before the event. Building standards enforced rather than merely written, restrictions on construction in exposed places, drainage maintained, warning systems that people have practised responding to, and titles registered so that assistance can reach the people entitled to it — these are undramatic, politically thankless, and produce a benefit that consists entirely of an absence. That is the recurring difficulty with prevention, and disasters are its clearest case.
